extracted.intended_audience: current and prospective peer reviewers for The BMJ (clinicians and researchers asked to review manuscripts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for clinicians and researchers performing peer review for The BMJ, covering administrative requirements (accepting invitations, open review, competing interests), the journal's publication priorities, ethical concerns, and how reviews may be used across the BMJ journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open (signed) peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ uses open peer review: reviewers have to sign their reports, saying briefly who they are and where they work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signing reports is mandatory; reviewers should include a brief identification. Open peer review does not permit authors to contact reviewers directly — all queries must go through the editorial office. If reviewers experience any adverse event arising from open peer review or wish to comment, they should email papersadmin@bmj.com.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaration of competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to declare to the editors any competing interests that might relate to articles we have asked them to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Declare any relevant financial, professional, or personal conflicts when asked. Use the journal/editorial office processes to report competing interests; see BMJ transparency policy for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to review invitations via the online editorial office
rubrics_metrics.description: If we need your help with appraising a manuscript we will email you and ask you to accept or reject the reviewing invitation at our online editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept or decline review invitations promptly through the online system so editors can allocate reviewers efficiently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise manuscripts according to BMJ aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should help prioritise manuscripts bearing in mind that the BMJ aims to publish original, important, and reliable articles that will help our readers around the world - who are mainly doctors - to make better decisions about practice, policy, education, and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appraising manuscripts focus on originality, importance, reliability, and practical value to clinicians and policy-makers. Use these priorities to advise editors on whether a submission merits publication in The BMJ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers advise; editors make final decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers advise the editors, who are responsible for the final decision to accept or reject a manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame reports as informed advice to editors rather than as binding decisions; include clear recommendations and rationale to help editorial decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviews and editorial comments may be transferred across BMJ journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors can nominate other BMJ Journals that they would like their manuscript to go to automatically if it is rejected by the first journal. The system also passes on editors' comments and peer reviewers' reports relating to that manuscript, to facilitate the review process at the next BMJ Journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that a review you write for The BMJ may later be seen by editors of other BMJ journals; write reports with the possibility of reuse/transfer in mind (clear, professional, and complete).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not contact reviewers/authors directly; use editorial office for queries
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review does not mean, however, that authors should feel able to contact reviewers directly to discuss their reports; all queries should still be directed through the editorial office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain communication via journal channels only. If an author seeks direct contact, refer them to the editorial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to other reviewers' reports after decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts sent for review are usually seen by at least two reviewers, and reviewers can access each other's reports on the same manuscript once the BMJ has made its decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that your report may be visible to other reviewers after the editorial decision; this provides feedback and learning opportunities—write reports that contribute constructively to this shared record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use BMJ transparency policy for ethics concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The BMJ transparency policy pulls together in one place many separate editorial policies. It's there, for example, that you'll find advice on what to do if you are concerned about the ethics aspects of a manuscript we have asked you to review or if you suspect plagiarism, duplicate publication, or scientific fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you suspect ethical problems (plagiarism, duplicate publication, fraud, or other ethics issues), consult the BMJ transparency policy for the correct procedures and report concerns through editorial channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article provenance statement
rubrics_metrics.description: At the end of every accepted editorial, research article, clinical review, practice article, analysis article, feature, and head-to-head article the BMJ will add a statement explaining the article's provenance. The options are: Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed; Not commissioned; not externally peer reviewed; Commissioned; externally peer reviewed; Commissioned; not externally peer reviewed; Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; externally peer reviewed; Commissioned, based on an idea from the author; not externally peer reviewed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that published articles will include a provenance statement indicating whether the piece was commissioned and/or externally peer reviewed; this is part of the journal's transparency practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording reviewing activity and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: To thank reviewers we offer a year’s online subscription to bmj.com and, if a reviewer already has access to bmj.com, we encourage them to pass this on to a colleague. We also provide reviewers with a Journal Activity Certificate for the BMJ. This keeps track of the work reviewers do for the BMJ and enables them to print off a certificate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Journal Activity Certificate to document reviewing for continuing professional development. Note the subscription benefit and consider passing it on if you already have access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feedback and peer review training
rubrics_metrics.description: We welcome feedback from our reviewers. ... Please note that we have an ongoing programme of editorial research and have, for example, conducted randomised controlled trials on open peer review and peer review training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide feedback on manuscripts and on the BMJ review process; consider using BMJ's peer review training materials and participating in related editorial research or training opportunities.
